Glimpse into a JS engineer's daily work (5-years experience)

The west, for the past 30-40 years, has been outsourcing their manufacturing jobs to countries in Asia. Some of the advantages of having jobs in these regions is that you can employ people for cheap, and construct and sell products for cheap. One of the major disadvantages of this though is that workers at home lose their jobs, which results in them getting unemployed, risking losing their house due to not paying mortgage or rent on it, going homeless, needing massive government assistance. You can thank free trade with significantly poorer countries for this, and in the future, automation of jobs.

I fear for the day when we start to see services jobs drop off like flies to be replaced, not with humans in other countries, but by robots who suddenly don't need to feed families, need to worry about healthcare, paying taxes, etc. Society ultimately loses when this happens, the only people that get the advantages of this are rich multinational companies who already rape our country by selling goods made by foreigners into a country that has only their services and (a small percentage of) knowledge, like America, but at this point, it could be for any western country. We are already seeing jobs being replaced with robots, at supermarkets you have self-service kiosks, in China there are self-driving buses, in America, Uber and Google are testing self-driving taxis, this is just a few jobs out of many that are being automated/replaced with robots. All of this is going to hurt western society, massively.

I feel that, in order for a robot tax to work, you need to get rid of free-trade deals with countries that earn much less than the west. I think western countries, which earn a similar wage overall, should have a free-trade deal with each other in order for this to work. What are some countries I'd have free-trade with, and what other countries would I scrap? I'd continue to have free-trade with South Korea, Japan and Singapore, I'd have free-trade with the five-eyes, France, Germany and of course, Israel. All of these countries share our values in common of liberal democracy, freedom and overall, similar wages. The countries I'd end free-trade with is China (but interestingly, in the future, when this would be enacted, their wage would be very similar to South Korea's or Japan's), Mexico, all of the middle-east (excluding Israel and Turkey, depending on how bad their current president fucks them). In order for free trade with these countries to work, you need to include a provision that says that they must have a robot tax that fits our definitions, else there is no agreement. There is no loss for these countries not to have a robot tax, their respective governments would get extra revenue, it makes producing stuff then shipping over to sell unaffordable suddenly, and the west for the most part, would see a boom in jobs, but I don't think this would be without a recession first from the shock of changing things, but in the long-term, I think we could see some real advantages come out of this.

What are some things I would consider a "robot?"

*Self-checkout kiosks

*Self-driving public transport (buses, taxis)

*Self-driving freight transport (trucks, trains)

*Automated masonry (massive threat to construction)

*Commercial 3D printers (manufacturing threat)

*Farming equipment which can pull and plant all kinds of produce and can feed and milk animals.

How would we know if someone has a robot or not? If you commercially order some technology, you must pay GST on it initially, once the government sees this, businesses should be asked to declare if they have any of the above (or more) and to pay a massive tax on each individual robot they have. If the average bloke in those jobs earns say $30,000/yr, you could say that the business/employer owes $35,000/machine to the government. This suddenly makes robots unaffordable to employers as you have to consider the initial purchasing cost, the GST paid on top of that, the cost of running robots, the cost of repairing them, etc. This could go well into $40k+/yr which makes humans $10k/yr cheaper than robots.

What are some issues I think could come out of this? I think the most important one is how you distinguish what a job-threatening robot is. If you leave it to vague, you will have issues, if it's too precise you will have issues. I believe without good explanation as to what a robot is you will have people confused therefore having negative economic impacts. The second most important is that a culture is created where people and sometimes companies are afraid of making things efficient in the sense that it could go under the guidelines of being a tax, when for example, all you want to do is to have a roller on the factory line instead of people pushing goods along to the dude who has to put in the next part.

What are your thoughts on this?

I feel like maybe we can have the tax remain just low enough for robots to still be competitive, then start putting that entirely towards a guaranteed minimum wage. That way, the replaced workers are still free to pursue other work, and the ones that can't find work will still have a buffer.

A guaranteed minimum wage, or something similar to a UBI, is very expensive. I want to avoid a UBI personally, that's why I recommend a robot tax, the goal is to continue to keep people employed that way they don't need to rely on government and the taxpayer (the number of which is decreasing). Let's do some calculations, the federal average minimum wage is about $7.50/hr * 8 hours a day * 5 days a week, that's already $300/week, now multiply that by the current population of America (330,000,000) that's $99,000,000,000 for a single week. Multiply that by 51 weeks in a year, $5.04900e12 /annually. Where do you get the tax payers to fund that programme alone if only 5% of the population were to be employed? That's the cost of a single programme, that's not including other aspects that you need to fund like the military, infrastructure construction, etc. This would result in extremely high taxes, which would result in inflation as the currency would be worth less since banks would be printing more, the demand of things would go up significantly, you get my point. I think a guaranteed minimum wage is nothing more than a pipe dream, unfortunately -- and this isn't including that different states have different minimum which are higher, therefore raising the overall cost of a guaranteed minimum wage by even more.
